entries.note: The claim is about 'potential' consequences and sets no measure for 'massive'. It states a possibility, not a firm outcome.

entries.test: Whether the Hofmann et al. paper found covert dialect prejudice in LLM outputs on consequential decision tasks such as employment and criminal judgments.
entries.note: The core of the claim is that the evidence exists, and it is hedged as grounds 'to suspect'. The opening remark that real-world use is unknown is vague.

entries.test: Whether the Hofmann et al. paper reported that human-feedback training failed to reduce covert dialect prejudice, or made it worse.
entries.note: 'I don't see an easy fix' is a personal view; the part that can be checked is what he says the paper showed. The paper reports that human feedback cut overt bias but not covert bias, which widened the gap between the two.
